stem.manager: How does the team decide whether a service is "reliable enough"?
stem.engineer: When someone asks you "Is the service healthy right now?", what do you base your answer on?

options.1: No clear indicators; we rely on user complaints or gut feeling
options.2: Basic monitoring (CPU, liveness checks), but no user-facing indicators
options.3: Core services have SLIs (success rate, latency, etc.) measured continuously
options.4: SLIs are derived from user journeys and regularly recalibrated against what users actually experience

stem.manager: What is the current state of your reliability targets?
stem.engineer: Do your core services have a target number? Has anyone compared it with reality?

options.1: No targets
options.2: "99.9%" is written down or said out loud, but nobody compares it with actual measurements
options.3: Core services have SLOs and dashboards, reviewed quarterly
options.4: SLOs are negotiated with product / business, adjusted based on data, and someone owns them

stem.manager: What role does the error budget play on the team?
stem.engineer: Have you seen the remaining error budget number? Where does it show up?

options.1: Never used it or never heard of it
options.2: We know the concept and have calculated it, but nobody looks at it
options.3: We calculate the remaining budget regularly and discuss it in review meetings
options.4: There is a written policy for when the budget runs out (e.g. a feature-release freeze), and it has actually been enforced

stem.manager: When did SLO or error budget data last change an actual decision?
stem.engineer: When do you remember last changing a schedule or approach because of an SLO number?

options.1: Never
options.2: More than a year ago, or I can't remember
options.3: Once in the past six months
options.4: Within the last quarter, and I can name the decision

stem.manager: How does the team operate when a major incident happens?
stem.engineer: The last time something broke at night or on a weekend, what happened in your first ten minutes on it?

options.1: Whoever notices handles it; no division of roles
options.2: There is on-call and an escalation path, but roles during the incident are decided on the spot
options.3: Severity levels, defined roles (incident commander, communications) and runbooks
options.4: Regular drills (game days); the process is revised based on drills and incident feedback

stem.manager: What does the team do after an incident is over?
stem.engineer: After an incident, what do the reviews you take part in look like?

options.1: A verbal discussion
options.2: Major incidents get a document, but it often stops at "human error"
options.3: A blameless format that finds systemic causes and produces action items
options.4: Action items have owners and deadlines, are tracked to closure, and are verified to be effective

stem.manager: How do lessons from incidents flow through the organization?
stem.engineer: Do you hear about other teams' incidents? Do you learn anything from them?

options.1: Only the people involved know
options.2: Documents exist, but few people read them
options.3: Regular cross-team sharing and reviews
options.4: Incident data is analyzed (recurring causes, MTTR trends) and shapes the roadmap

stem.manager: How much of the action items from the last major incident have been completed?
stem.engineer: As far as you know, how much of the action items from the last major incident have been completed?

options.1: No action items were produced
options.2: Less than 30%
options.4: More than 70%, and their effectiveness was verified

stem.manager: What are the team's observability capabilities?
stem.engineer: When something breaks, how many tools do you have to open to find the cause?

options.1: We log into machines and read logs
options.2: There are metrics dashboards, but logs are scattered and we dig through several places
options.3: Metrics, logs and traces can be correlated; core services have standard dashboards
options.4: We can drill down from a user symptom to the root cause; new services ship with standard observability by default

stem.manager: What are alerts mainly based on?
stem.engineer: When your phone goes off, what kind of alert is it usually?

options.1: Mostly infrastructure alerts (high CPU, etc.), often ignored
options.2: Alerts have severities, but there is a lot of noise; experience tells us which to ignore
options.3: Mainly based on user impact / symptoms; every alert has a runbook
options.4: Alerts are tied to SLO burn rate, and ineffective alerts are cleaned up regularly

q11.title: Actionable alert rate

stem.manager: Over the past month, what share of the team's pages actually needed someone to act?
stem.engineer: Of the pages you get on call, what share actually need you to act?

options.1: Less than 25%
options.4: 80% or more

q11.unsure: We don't track it, and I don't know

stem.manager: What is the current state of the release process?
stem.engineer: In your last release, what did the path from merge to production look like?

options.1: Manual deployments based on personal experience
options.2: CI/CD exists, but there are many manual checks before release, bunched into a few time slots
options.3: Automated deployment, progressive delivery (canary, blue-green), fast rollback
options.4: Release risk adjusts dynamically with SLOs / error budget; anomalies are detected and rolled back automatically

stem.manager: How does change management work?
stem.engineer: When something breaks, how quickly can you find out "what changed recently"?

options.1: Changes are not recorded
options.2: There are change tickets, but they're a formality and don't match actual deployments
options.3: Changes are traceable and can be linked to incidents
options.4: Change failure rate is measured and used to improve the process

stem.manager: For the last incident caused by a change, how long did it take from detection to recovery?
stem.engineer: For the last change-induced incident you went through, how long did it take from detection to recovery?

options.1: More than 4 hours
options.2: 1 to 4 hours
options.3: 15 to 60 minutes
options.4: Within 15 minutes (including automatic rollback)

stem.manager: How does the team view and manage repetitive operational work?
stem.engineer: How much of your week goes to repetitive, manual work with no lasting value? Is anyone measuring it?

options.1: Nobody distinguishes operational chores from engineering work
options.2: Everyone feels there is a lot, but it isn't quantified
options.3: Toil share is measured from tickets / on-call records, with a target cap
options.4: Fixed engineering time is reserved to eliminate toil, and the reduction is tracked

stem.manager: What is the current state of automation?
stem.engineer: How are common operational tasks done today?

options.1: Personal scripts and word of mouth
options.2: Scripts exist but are scattered and barely maintained
options.3: Repetitive tasks have shared, version-controlled automation; IaC is the default
options.4: Self-service: service owners can do common operations without filing a ticket

stem.manager: Which piece of repetitive work did the team eliminate last quarter?
stem.engineer: As far as you know, which piece of repetitive work did the team eliminate last quarter?

options.1: None, or I can't recall
options.2: One or two, handled in passing
options.3: Planned into a sprint and completed
options.4: Hours saved were quantified and are tracked over time

stem.manager: How is service ownership defined?
stem.engineer: If your service breaks at night, who should be woken up? Does everyone agree?

options.1: Nobody is clearly responsible; we call whoever knows it best
options.2: There is a service list, but owners are often out of date
options.3: Every core service has a clear owner and an on-call rotation shared by the development team
options.4: Services must pass entry criteria (production readiness review) to launch, and owners are accountable for reliability

stem.manager: How is on-call load managed?
stem.engineer: What is your on-call experience like?

options.1: A few people carry it for long stretches
options.2: There is a rotation, but people are often woken at night and fatigue is obvious
options.3: The rotation is fair, there is time off in lieu, and night pages are tracked
options.4: On-call load is a management metric; exceeding limits triggers changes (fewer alerts, more people)

stem.manager: The last time reliability and feature delivery conflicted, how was it decided?
stem.engineer: The most recent reliability vs. feature delivery conflict you know of — how was it decided?

options.1: No mechanism; the loudest voice wins
options.2: A manager decides on the spot; reliability usually gives way
options.3: There is a data-based discussion, but it isn't binding
options.4: There is a pre-agreed policy (error budget policy), and reliability work has been prioritized because of it
